text.title: Futures sink as AI sell-off resumes and new tariff plans hit; Nasdaq 100 futures down 2.8%
text.summary: US stock futures point to a sharply lower open: S&P 500 futures are down 1.9%, Nasdaq 100 futures 2.8%, Dow futures 1.3% and Russell 2000 futures 1.2%. The VIX jumped 16.3% to 30.65. Technology is again the epicenter, with Nvidia and Anthropic leading a global tech sell-off, and a new US tariff proposal on 14 trading partners adds trade risk. Treasury yields are little changed (10-year at 4.90%) while the dollar edged up 0.2%, so bonds are offering only modest shelter. Gold fell 1.4% and bitcoin 1.8%, so the pressure is broad across risk assets. Core PCE inflation and GDP data at 8:30 AM ET are the next test.
text.rates: The 10-year Treasury yield is 4.90%, down 2 bp, and the 2-year is unchanged at 4.63%. Both are about 25 bp below their one-month highs, so yields have eased even as stocks fall. Bloomberg describes investors turning to bonds for safety, but tightening expectations limit how far yields can fall. The dollar index is up 0.2% to 104.0, which tends to weigh on commodities and multinational earnings. WTI oil is up 0.5% to $82.46 but remains about 19% below its one-month high. Gold's 1.4% drop shows it is not acting as a haven today.
text.breadth: Overseas, the tech sell-off dominated: Japan's Nikkei fell 2.8% and Hong Kong's Hang Seng 1.9%. In Europe the Euro Stoxx 50 lost 0.6% and the DAX 0.3%, while the FTSE 100 was flat as defensive stocks offset weakness, with US inflation data and tariffs looming. Bloomberg notes tech underperformed in Europe. The pattern points to a risk-off open in the US, with tech under the most pressure.
text.context: The S&P 500 is 7.0% below its one-month high and the Nasdaq 10.6% below, with the VIX up about 67% over the month. The Dow and Russell 2000 had risen two straight sessions before today's drop. J.P. Morgan's weekly recap notes the S&P 500 fell about 8.6% in the week to Nov 20, with growth stocks down more than value; year to date, large-cap growth was down 13.6% and large-cap value up 18.9% as of that date.
text.takeaway: Sharp, tech-led drawdowns are a normal if uncomfortable part of equity investing, and diversified portfolios are built with them in mind. Spreading exposure across sectors, regions and asset classes helps limit the impact of any one theme reversing.
text.talk: Markets are lower this morning as the AI-related tech sell-off continues and new tariff proposals add uncertainty. Inflation and GDP data due at 8:30 AM ET will help show how the economy is holding up.

drivers.t: Futures tumbled as the AI sell-off returned, with Nvidia and Anthropic leading the way. Bloomberg reports that the euphoria after CEO Jensen Huang's return on Monday is fading as questions over the chipmaker linger. A global tech sell-off shows no sign of letting up, with investors turning to bonds. Tech is the most heavily weighted and richly valued corner of the index, so shifting AI sentiment moves it most. Nasdaq 100 futures are down 2.8% after the Nasdaq fell 1.5% yesterday, and Japan's Nikkei dropped 2.8% overnight.

drivers.h: Washington adds tariff and political risk
drivers.t: The US proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU, targeting trade practices it deems unfair. Tariffs raise input costs and invite retaliation, which can squeeze margins and cloud the global growth outlook. Copper is heading for one of its worst months in over a decade as tariff uncertainty weighs on demand. Nvidia is also drawing bipartisan scrutiny over its ties to the administration, and Huang's return has fueled a Washington fight over China chip access. This adds a policy overhang to a stock already under pressure.

drivers.h: Tightening fears keep the dollar firm
drivers.t: Societe Generale says the dollar firmed on expectations of aggressive Fed tightening to bring growth back to trend and inflation under control. Bloomberg reports bond traders are hedging a 'hike now, cut later' scenario, with a risk that higher rates make the economy stumble. Higher rate expectations raise the discount rate on future earnings, which typically hurts long-duration growth stocks most. The dollar index is up 0.2% to 104.0. The 10-year yield is 4.90%, down 2 bp, and has fallen 20 bp over five days.

A MarketWatch strategist argues that liquidity has peaked, with bitcoin falling first, then gold and now stocks. Today's moves fit that pattern: gold is down 1.4% to 3,541.3 and has fallen 5.4% in five days, and bitcoin is down 1.8% and about 27% below its one-month high. When safe havens and speculative assets fall together, forced selling and deleveraging are often at work, not a single catalyst. MarketWatch also notes the S&P 500 has slid through a key trendline again, with no V-shaped recovery this time. That may keep technically driven selling in focus.

Higher food, travel and gift costs are pressuring holiday budgets, with inflation and Iran-war energy shocks cited. US food inflation is returning, which makes the Thanksgiving meal costlier. MarketWatch notes October's spending report will show how much Americans are actually buying heading into Black Friday. Sticky prices squeeze discretionary spending and complicate the inflation picture. That is why today's Core PCE print is closely watched.

earnings.t: Dell is down 5.8% pre-market despite beating on earnings and revenue, which suggests the AI sell-off is outweighing the results. MarketWatch notes Dell checks whether its AI customers have enough electricity.

watch.why: The forecast is 3.5% versus 3.4% previously, and strong growth could reinforce expectations of tighter policy.
The scope and timing of the levies on China and the EU will shape trade and growth expectations.
It will show how much consumers are actually buying heading into Black Friday.
